params.title: Environment-Wide WMI→PowerShell→rundll32 Attack Chain Across 4+ Systems
Cross-System Data Theft Operation: R&D Intellectual Property Staged for Exfiltration via perfmon Directories
Domain Credential Compromise: Registry Hive Extraction and rsydow-a Account Used for Environment-Wide Lateral Movement
Convergent Connections to 172.16.4.10:8080 — McAfee ePO Management Traffic, Not C2
params.description:
Network scan analysis across multiple memory dumps reveals convergent outbound connections to 172.16.4.10:8080 from at least four different systems: base-rd-01 (172.16.7.11), base-hunt (172.16.5.25), base-hunt-db (172.16.5.20), and 172.16.7.15. 

**Re-assessment: This is legitimate McAfee ePO management traffic, NOT C2.**

Evidence supporting the McAfee ePO interpretation:
1. macmnsvc.exe (McAfee Common Management Agent) is listening on port 8081 on multiple hosts — the ePO server at 172.16.4.10:8080 is the management console
2. chrome.exe on 172.16.5.20 connecting to both 172.16.4.10:8080 and :80 is consistent with accessing the ePO web console via browser
3. base-wkstn-05 registry explicitly configures 172.16.4.10:8080 as HTTP Proxy (McAfee ePO proxy setting)
4. Every system with a memory dump shows McAfee Agent processes (masvc.exe, macmnsvc.exe, macompatsvc.exe) — this is the standard management channel
5. The subject_srv.exe connection was previously misattributed; it is confirmed F-Response (not related to 172.16.4.10 traffic)

This convergent pattern represents legitimate enterprise security management infrastructure, not command-and-control.

params.title: DMZ-to-Internal Attack Path: External FTP Compromise Concurrent with Internal WMI Lateral Movement
p.exe (c:\windows\temp\perfmon\p.exe) — Confirmed Malware Implant with Massive RWX Memory on base-rd-01/base-admin
params.description:
Cross-system confirmation: p.exe (PID 8260) is the primary malware payload in the WMI attack chain, running from c:\windows\temp\perfmon\p.exe. Key evidence convergence:

1. **Volatility malfind**: 481 pages of PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE memory — far beyond any legitimate application
2. **Volatility cmdline**: Launched via cmd.exe /C (PID 5948, PPID 5848/powershell.exe) at 2018-08-30 22:15:18
3. **Volatility dlllist**: Loaded ADVAPI32.dll, sechost.dll, RPCRT4.dll — standard Windows APIs for service/registry interaction
4. **Volatility psscan**: Active from 2018-08-30 through memory capture with 2 threads
5. **Volatility netscan (base-rd-01)**: Associated system had SMB connections to multiple internal hosts
6. **Registry ShimCache**: Same perfmon directory used for ri.exe on BASE-MAIL, linking to same threat actor

p.exe spawned multiple rundll32.exe instances over 7 days (2018-08-30 to 2018-09-06), indicating persistent C2 capability. The massive 481-page RWX allocation suggests a packed/encrypted payload that decrypts in memory — consistent with a RAT/implant. Binary analysis was not performed due to the evidence being a memory dump without separate disk extraction.

params.title: Nmap NSE Scan from DMZ Host 172.16.10.13 and WebDAV Admin Share Probe from 172.16.5.26
params.description:
Two internal hosts conducted suspicious reconnaissance against the DMZ FTP server (172.16.10.12):

**Nmap scan from 172.16.10.13 (2018-09-04 17:37-17:38):**
- GET / on ports 80/443, then Nmap NSE probes: /sdk (VMware), /HNAP1 (router), /evox/about (device), /nmaplowercheck* (service detection)
- The scan originated from within the DMZ subnet (172.16.10.0/24), suggesting either a compromised DMZ host or an authorized security scan
- Timing falls between external FTP reconnaissance (Sep 2-3) and authenticated access (Sep 5)

**WebDAV probes from 172.16.5.26 (2018-09-07 02:46-05:21):**
- OPTIONS / → 200, OPTIONS /c$ → 200 (admin share probe), OPTIONS /srl-ftp → 200
- Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.16299 user-agent (Windows 10)
- 172.16.5.26 is the same host that previously authenticated to FTP as nfury and dblake on 2018-08-07

The /c$ probe is notable — accessing the C: administrative share via WebDAV on a DMZ server would bypass FTP authentication. The 200 OPTIONS response indicates WebDAV was enabled on IIS but doesn't confirm file access.

Memory analysis of base-rd-02 (172.16.6.12) reveals two processes with names mimicking Microsoft's advapi32.dll running as Windows services:

**msadvapi2_64.exe (PID 2328):** PPID 760/services.exe, SessionId 0, native 64-bit, started 2018-08-19 06:23:13 (boot time), 5 threads
**msadvapi2_32.exe (PID 2292):** PPID 760/services.exe, SessionId 0, Wow64=True (32-bit), started 2018-08-19 06:23:13 (boot time), 5 threads

**Cross-system correlation shows this is unique to base-rd-02** — these binaries were NOT found on any other system's memory dump or disk image (DC, file server, base-rd-01, base-wkstn-01, base-wkstn-05). Combined with the WMI→PowerShell attack chain also identified on base-rd-02 (PID 6528, 2018-09-06 17:10:53), plus extensive sc.exe and netstat.exe reconnaissance, base-rd-02 shows signs of both pre-existing persistence (msadvapi2 at boot since Aug 19) and new WMI exploitation (Sep 6).

The dual-architecture deployment (32-bit + 64-bit), masquerading names, boot-time persistence, and absence from other systems strongly suggest these are attacker-deployed implants or unauthorized monitoring tools. Binary analysis is recommended to confirm.

params.title: WMI Lateral Movement and Fileless Execution on base-av — Same Attack Chain as base-rd-01
params.description:
Cross-system correlation confirms the same WMI→PowerShell→rundll32 attack chain on base-av as on base-rd-01 and base-wkstn-01:

WmiPrvSE.exe (PID 2676) → powershell.exe (PID 3920) → powershell.exe 32-bit (PID 1332, Wow64=True, 2018-08-31 01:31:25, 10 threads, 655 handles) → rundll32.exe (PID 5056, exited) + persistent rundll32.exe (PID 7100, 5 threads, 337 handles, still running at capture, started 2018-08-31 18:43:50).

This is the SAME technique and timing as the chains on base-rd-01 (2018-08-30 16:43) and base-wkstn-01 (2018-08-31 01:14-01:31), confirming environment-wide compromise by a single threat actor. McAfee HIPS (HipMgmt.exe PID 1572) was present but did not prevent the attack. The persistent rundll32 PID 7100 with 5 threads and 337 handles indicates sustained attacker access at the time of memory acquisition.

params.title: ShimCache Evidence: System Provisioning Entries (2017-09-29) Plus Attacker UNC Path Access (2018-08-31 to 2018-09-05)
params.description:
ShimCache/AppCompatCache entries from base-rd-01 contain two distinct categories of evidence:

**CATEGORY 1 — System Provisioning (NOT attacker activity):**
All entries dated 2017-09-29 (13:41-13:43) are consistent with Windows system imaging/provisioning. The same 2-minute window shows dozens of executables being touched, including sysprep.exe, shutdown.exe, disksnapshot.exe, SETUPUGC.EXE, oobe tools, svchost.exe, regedit.exe, dfrgui.exe, winsat.exe, and many Windows Store app registrations. This is a standard system installation/configuration signature. The following tools ARE part of provisioning, NOT attacker tool usage:
- quser.exe, find.exe, schtasks.exe, sc.exe, reg.exe, netsh.exe, cmd.exe, DllHost.exe, taskmgr.exe
- All timestamped 2017-09-29, approximately 11 months before the incident

**CATEGORY 2 — Attacker Tool Access (September 2018):**
The ShimCache also records confirmed attacker activity:
- \\\\172.16.4.6\\c$\\Windows\\Temp\\perfmon\\ri.exe (2018-09-05 14:05:51) — same perfmon staging directory as p.exe
- \\\\172.16.4.6\\c$\\Windows\\Logs\\WindowsServerBackup\\6.14\\volrest.exe (2018-08-31 23:28:16)
These UNC path accesses via administrative shares (C$) are covered in detail in finding f_a6780b9f.

**Counter-analysis note (Q7):** The original finding implied the 2017-09-29 ShimCache entries showed "attacker tool execution." This is incorrect — the timestamps and co-occurrence with system provisioning utilities conclusively identify these as imaging artifacts. Only the September 2018 UNC path entries represent attacker activity. Title and MITRE tags updated accordingly.

The SECURITY registry hive was found copied to `\temp\registry\SECURITY` (MFT entry 132834, size 65536 bytes) with a creation timestamp of 2018-09-05 12:17:02. Copying the SECURITY hive to a temporary directory is consistent with credential harvesting techniques (T1003.002/T1003.004) — the SECURITY hive contains LSA secrets, cached credentials, and the SAM database encryption key.

**Counter-analysis note (Q2):** The IR team was demonstrably active before this event: Autorunsc was executed on 2018-08-15, and Plaso acquisition was running on base-wkstn-01 since 2018-08-29 — both BEFORE the WMI attack chain started on 2018-08-30. The SECURITY hive copy on 2018-09-05 could therefore be IR-related forensic collection (e.g., `reg save HKLM\SECURITY`) rather than attacker credential harvesting.

**Arguments for attacker activity:** (1) The `\temp\registry\` path is non-standard for IR tools, which typically use dedicated output directories. (2) Only the SECURITY hive was found — IR collection typically captures SAM, SYSTEM, and SOFTWARE as well. (3) The timing (2018-09-05 12:17:02) coincides with active attack operations: p.exe spawned rundll32 at 2018-09-05 12:01:32, and ri.exe was accessed at 14:05:51 the same day. (4) The R&D data staging on the DC occurred in the `\Temp\perfmon\` directory (2018-08-31), establishing attacker presence in the DC's temp directories.

**Arguments for IR activity:** (1) IR team was already active. (2) Forensic analysts commonly use `reg save` to collect hives. (3) The `\temp\registry\` path could be ad-hoc IR collection.

Assessment: Retaining as HIGH severity / inference confidence given the convergent attack activity on the same day and the non-standard path, but the IR collection alternative cannot be ruled out.

params.title: Malfind Hits in SQL Server Components on base-hunt — Confirmed Benign CLR JIT
params.description:
Multiple Volatility malfind hits were detected in SQL Server-related processes on the base-hunt/database system (IP 172.16.5.20):

- MsDtsSrvr.exe (PID 1208): 4 VadS regions with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE
- msmdsrv.exe (PID 1348): 4 VadS regions
- ReportingServi (PID 1920): 6 VadS regions
- sqlceip.exe (PIDs 1180, 2080, 2184): Multiple regions each
- Microsoft.Repo (PID 2052): 4 VadS regions

The byte patterns `I\xc7\xc2` (mov r10, imm) and `H\xb8` (mov rax, imm) followed by `\xff\xe0` (jmp rax) are characteristic of .NET CLR JIT compilation stubs. These are expected for SQL Server components which use the .NET runtime extensively. No suspicious parent-child relationships or network connections were associated with these processes.

**Counter-analysis note:** Downgraded from MEDIUM to INFO. The finding's own conclusion states these are "likely false positives caused by legitimate .NET CLR JIT memory allocations." When a finding concludes benign, its severity should match that assessment. MITRE tags removed as these do not represent process injection or PowerShell execution.

The base-hunt system (IP 172.16.5.26, memory captured 2018-07-29) shows extensive remote access activity:

**PuTTY Sessions**: Six concurrent putty.exe instances were running (PIDs 7368, 2516, 4456, 2092, 12844, 14596), all spawned from explorer.exe (PID 3156), indicating interactive user-driven SSH sessions. The earliest was created 2018-07-31 14:44:29 (PID 7368) and the latest 2018-08-10 15:38:40 (PID 14596).

**WinRM Connection Evidence**: Network scan reveals WinRM connections to 172.16.5.21:5985, indicating Windows Remote Management for remote command execution.

**SMB/File Share Access**: ESTABLISHED TCP connection from 172.16.5.26:52182 → 172.16.4.5:445 (SMB to infrastructure host).

**External Connection**: rubyw.exe (PID 3800) connecting to 10.10.254.1:61613 (ActiveMQ/STOMP), consistent with Puppet/MCollective infrastructure management.

**Counter-analysis note:** Downgraded from MEDIUM to LOW. The base-hunt system (172.16.5.25/26) is confirmed as the forensic investigation workstation — it is the F-Response server that all subject_srv.exe agents report to (base-hunt.shieldbase.lan:5682), and it runs tools like Autorunsc and Plaso. Multiple PuTTY sessions, WinRM connections, and SMB access are EXPECTED behavior for an IR/admin workstation managing an active forensic investigation. The volume of concurrent sessions reflects the multi-system investigation, not suspicious pivoting. The MITRE techniques for legitimate admin/SSH use from the IR workstation are over-attributed.

Memory analysis of base-rd-02 (172.16.6.12) reveals two processes with names mimicking Microsoft's advapi32.dll running as Windows services:

**msadvapi2_64.exe (PID 2328):** PPID 760/services.exe, SessionId 0, native 64-bit, started 2018-08-19 06:23:13 (boot time), 5 threads
**msadvapi2_32.exe (PID 2292):** PPID 760/services.exe, SessionId 0, Wow64=True (32-bit), started 2018-08-19 06:23:13 (boot time), 5 threads

**Cross-system correlation shows this is unique to base-rd-02** — these binaries were NOT found on any other system. Combined with the WMI→PowerShell attack chain also identified on base-rd-02, the system shows signs of both pre-existing persistence and new WMI exploitation.

**Counter-analysis note (Q3):** The boot-time start (2018-08-19) predates the WMI attack by 11 days, and the dual-architecture deployment pattern (32+64 bit) COULD be consistent with a legitimate monitoring or management agent. Their DLL loads and network connections have not been examined, and binary analysis was not performed. However, the following factors maintain the HIGH/inference rating: (1) The naming convention "msadvapi2" clearly masquerades as Microsoft's advapi32.dll — a technique associated with T1036.005. (2) Legitimate enterprise tools are typically deployed across multiple systems, not on a single host. (3) No other system in the environment runs these binaries. (4) The Puppet configuration management on base-rd-02 could theoretically deploy niche agents, but such tools would typically have recognizable vendor names.

Binary analysis of these executables is needed to resolve this conclusively. If they are a legitimate tool, their deployment path through Puppet and their vendor should be identifiable.

YARA scanning of the DC memory dump produced 233+ rule matches. Analysis reveals these are predominantly generic string matches: APT6_Malware_Sample_Gen matched on common strings like C:\WINDOWS\system32\, synflood, udpflood, and shellcode. Multiple matches on Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved. are from legitimate Microsoft binaries. These matches are consistent with over-matching by broad YARA signatures against a Windows Server memory image containing many system binaries. No specific high-confidence malware signatures were confirmed.

**Counter-analysis note (Q10):** This finding overlaps substantially with f_09a5da7e and f_535e676e, which document the same APT6_Malware_Sample_Gen over-matching issue from different analysis perspectives. All three findings reach the same conclusion: the APT6 rule matches are false positives from generic Windows strings. See f_535e676e for the consolidated cross-system view. Retained as the initial DC-specific assessment.

YARA scanning of the DC memory dump produced 466 match windows across both memory dump instances, primarily from the `APT6_Malware_Sample_Gen` rule. Analysis of the matched strings shows these are false positives matching on common, legitimate strings present in any Windows memory dump:

**Matched strings (all generic/benign):**
- $s3: "C:\\WINDOWS\\system32\\" - Standard Windows system path
- $s9: synflood - Common networking term in TCP/IP stack
- $s11: udpflood - Common networking term
- $s12: shellcode - Common term in security software signatures
- $f: ServiceMain - Standard Windows service API function
- $n1: file:// - Standard URL scheme
- $c7: \\sysprep - Standard Windows system prep tool
- $x2: "Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved." - Standard copyright string

**Counter-analysis note (Q10):** This finding is redundant with f_875b55ac (initial DC assessment) and f_535e676e (cross-system consolidated view). All three conclude APT6 YARA matches are false positives. This finding provides the most detailed string-by-string analysis but the conclusion is identical across all three. Similarly, f_8826b9c2 documents Snake/Turla YARA false positives from the same category of over-matching on generic strings and file extensions.

Two internal hosts conducted reconnaissance against the DMZ FTP server (172.16.10.12):

**Nmap scan from 172.16.10.13 (2018-09-04 17:37-17:38):**
- GET / on ports 80/443, then Nmap NSE probes: /sdk (VMware), /HNAP1 (router), /evox/about (device), /nmaplowercheck* (service detection)
- The scan originated from within the DMZ subnet (172.16.10.0/24), suggesting either a compromised DMZ host or an authorized security scan
- Timing falls between external FTP reconnaissance (Sep 2-3) and authenticated access (Sep 5)

**WebDAV probes from 172.16.5.26 (2018-09-07 02:46-05:21):**
- OPTIONS / → 200, OPTIONS /c$ → 200 (admin share probe), OPTIONS /srl-ftp → 200
- Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.16299 user-agent (Windows 10)
- 172.16.5.26 is the same host that previously authenticated to FTP as nfury and dblake on 2018-08-07

**Counter-analysis note (Q9):** The Nmap scan from 172.16.10.13 could be from an authorized vulnerability scanner or security appliance within the DMZ. NSE probes for /sdk (VMware), /HNAP1 (router), and /evox (device detection) are standard service-discovery scripts run by security scanners, not targeted exploitation. However, the timing between external recon and authenticated access prevents ruling out attacker pivoting. The WebDAV probes from 172.16.5.26 (base-hunt — the IR workstation) at 2018-09-07 are more likely IR team investigation activity, consistent with the IR team checking FTP server configuration during the incident response. The /c$ OPTIONS request is a common IR check to verify whether administrative shares are exposed via WebDAV.

questions_addressed: Q1: WMI chains on 4 systems are NOT McAfee ePO — distinct technique (PowerShell 32-bit downstage + rundll32), distinct parent (WmiPrvSE not ManagementAgent), distinct systems. No change needed.
Q2: SECURITY hive copy COULD be IR collection — updated f_a015a6f7 with counter-arguments. Retained HIGH/inference because same-day attack activity and non-standard path lean toward attacker.

Q3: msadvapi2 binaries COULD be legitimate — updated f_a0fa91fe with counter-arguments. Retained HIGH/inference because name masquerading and single-system deployment are suspicious. Binary analysis needed.
Q4: rsydow-f FTP access pattern (failed nfury → navigate rsydow-f → authenticate 2 days later) is consistent with credential discovery/exploitation. No downgrade.
Q5: Orocobre PDF in perfmon directory is attacker staging — same naming convention as malware staging, on DC (not user workstation), in Windows\Temp (not user directory). No change.
Q6: IR team active before attack — incorporated into f_a015a6f7 and f_438137a8. Suggests either earlier undetected attack phase or routine baseline that coincidentally preceded attack.
Q7: ShimCache 2017-09-29 entries are system provisioning — updated f_e35b7f08 to clearly distinguish provisioning from attacker activity. MITRE tags removed from provisioning entries.
Q8: f_438137a8 downgraded from HIGH to INFO — system profile finding, not a threat indicator. MITRE tags removed.
Q9: Nmap from 172.16.10.13 could be authorized scanner — updated f_9a39ae05 with counter-argument. WebDAV from 172.16.5.26 is likely IR team. Retained MEDIUM/inference.
Q10: Three YARA APT6 findings are redundant — annotated all three with cross-references. Not merged to preserve analysis trail but redundancy documented.
